bullets: Two graphs can describe the same journey - but each graph answers a different question
slides.heading: A-Math kinematics: reading motion from s–t and v–t graphs
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we read displacement-time and velocity-time graphs for the same motion, find velocity from a gradient, find displacement from an area, meet the SUVAT pair, and expose the trap of reading a straight s-t graph as acceleration.

bullets: Read the velocity of a motion as the gradient of its s-t graph and the displacement as the area under its v-t graph
Use the SUVAT pair v = u + at and s = ut + (1/2)at^2 for motion with constant acceleration
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things, including spotting the straight-line gradient trap.

bullets: A car moves in a straight line and its journey is drawn twice: once as s against t, once as v against t
The s-t line climbs steadily while the v-t line sits flat - so is the car speeding up, or not?
slides.heading: One journey, two graphs - which one tells the speed?
slides.notes: Ask the class to vote: is this car speeding up? Take two or three answers, then point out that the two graphs describe one motion, and each must be read on its own terms.

bullets: The gradient of an s-t graph is the velocity: gradient = change in displacement divided by change in time
The area under a v-t graph is the displacement: each thin strip is velocity times a small time step
For constant acceleration, v = u + at and s = ut + (1/2)at^2 link velocity, displacement, acceleration and time
slides.heading: Gradient and area: the two readings
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: a graph gives up its meaning through its gradient or its area - gradient of s-t is velocity, gradient of v-t is acceleration, area under v-t is displacement.

bullets: The s-t line is straight: displacement grows evenly, so the motion is uniform
The v-t line is flat at the same time: the speed never changes, so the velocity is constant
slides.heading: Two graphs, one motion
slides.notes: Point at the animation and narrate: watch the two dots move together - the climbing dot on the s-t graph and the level dot on the v-t graph are the same journey.

bullets: Pick two points on the s-t graph and build the gradient triangle: rise in displacement over run in time
For the points (0, 10) and (6, 40) the gradient is (40 - 10)/(6 - 0) = 5, so the velocity is 5 m/s
slides.heading: Gradient of the s–t graph is the velocity
slides.notes: Follow the probe as it builds the gradient triangle and name each leg: the run is the time between the points, the rise is the change in displacement, and rise over run is the velocity.

bullets: Each thin rectangle under the v-t curve is velocity times a small time step - a small distance
Stacking the rectangles fills the area under the curve, and that total area is the displacement
slides.heading: Area under the v–t graph is the displacement
slides.notes: Watch the sweep lay down one thin rectangle at a time: speed times a small time is a small distance, and the stacked rectangles are the displacement - displacement is the integral of velocity.

bullets: Under constant acceleration a, velocity is v = u + at and displacement is s = ut + (1/2)at^2
The trap claim is: A straight s-t graph means constant acceleration.
slides.heading: The SUVAT pair — and the gradient trap
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud before anyone falls into it: a straight s-t graph has constant gradient, the gradient of s-t is velocity, so the velocity is constant and the acceleration is zero.

bullets: Step 1: read two points on the s-t line: (0, 10) and (6, 40)
Step 2: gradient = (40 - 10)/(6 - 0) = 5, so the velocity is 5 m/s, constant along the whole line
slides.heading: Worked example: velocity from an s-t gradient
slides.notes: Talk through the two steps slowly: pick points that are easy to read, form rise over run, and attach the unit metres per second to the answer.

bullets: Find the velocity from the s-t graph provided and the displacement from the area under the v-t graph provided
Careful - a classmate claims: A straight s-t graph means constant acceleration. Explain to them what a straight s-t graph really says about the velocity and the acceleration
slides.heading: Your turn: read the graphs, then check the trap
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call two pairs: listen for the trap - A straight s-t graph means constant acceleration. The fix is: The gradient of s-t is velocity: a straight s-t graph has constant velocity and zero acceleration.

bullets: On your own: state the velocity shown by a straight s-t graph through (0, 10) and (6, 40)
Watch out for the trap one last time: A straight s-t graph means constant acceleration. Say what the gradient of the s-t graph actually measures
slides.heading: Exit ticket: prove it before you leave
slides.notes: Close by reminding the class of the trap - A straight s-t graph means constant acceleration. - and the fix: The gradient of s-t is velocity: a straight s-t graph has constant velocity and zero acceleration. Collect the tickets as they leave and check who still reads a straight s-t line as acceleration.
